articles.headline: Growing Life in Zero-G: The Science Behind China's 'Fake' Embryo Experiment in Space
articles.summary:
Imagine trying to build a complex puzzle while floating in mid-air—that's essentially what China is trying to understand at the cellular level with its latest space mission. Recently, China launched synthetic human embryos to its Tiangong space station. But don't worry, these aren't actual human babies in the making. They are 'embryoids'—tiny, 3D clusters of stem cells that mimic the very earliest stages of a human embryo. Scientists use these lab-grown stand-ins to study life's beginnings without crossing the heavy ethical boundaries of experimenting on real human embryos.

The core scientific puzzle here is how microgravity—the near-weightless environment of space—affects the most fundamental steps of life. On Earth, gravity is a silent architect. As an embryo grows from a single cell into a cluster of cells, and as those cells start folding and organizing into tissues and organs, gravity is constantly pulling on them. Without that downward pull in space, do the cells still know where to go? Do they divide and organize correctly, or does zero-G throw the whole blueprint off?

By sending these embryoids to the Tiangong space station, researchers can watch this microscopic drama unfold in real time. If the synthetic embryos develop normally, it’s a promising sign that the basic mechanics of human development don't strictly require Earth's gravity. However, if they grow abnormally or fail to organize, it could mean that gravity is a much more crucial ingredient for human life than we ever realized.

The implications of this experiment stretch far beyond the lab. If humanity ever wants to become a multi-planetary species—setting up bases on the Moon or traveling to Mars—we need to know if we can safely reproduce in space. This research is the very first step in answering the ultimate sci-fi question: can we make space babies? By blending cutting-edge stem cell science with space exploration, China's mission isn't just about studying cells; it's about testing the limits of human survival among the stars.

sources.title: China just launched fake human embryos to its space station for a new research mission

articles.headline: Shattering the Cosmic Mirror: How Yang Zhenning's Nobel-Winning Discovery Changed Physics Forever
articles.summary:
Imagine looking at your reflection in a mirror. If you raise your right hand, your reflection raises its left. For a long time, physicists believed the universe worked exactly the same way: the laws of nature were perfectly symmetric, meaning a mirror-image universe would operate identically to our own. This foundational concept was known as 'parity conservation,' the idea that nature does not favor left over right.
In the 1950s, physicists were baffled by a cosmic puzzle involving particles called kaons, which seemed to behave identically in every way except how they decayed. Yang Zhenning and Li Zhengdao proposed a radical solution: what if the laws of nature are NOT mirror-symmetric? They hypothesized that in the 'weak interaction'—the fundamental force responsible for radioactive decay—parity might not be conserved. This meant that under certain conditions, nature actually does have a directional preference, and a mirrored universe would behave differently from ours.
Proving this required a masterful experiment, which was conducted by physicist Chien-Shiung Wu. She observed the radioactive decay of cobalt-60 atoms in extremely cold conditions. If parity were conserved, the electrons emitted during decay would fly out equally in all directions relative to the atoms' spin. Instead, Wu found that the electrons had a strong preference for one specific direction! If you watched this process in a mirror, the reflection would violate the actual laws of physics. The universe, it turned out, is fundamentally 'left-handed.'
This discovery sent shockwaves through the scientific community, overturning a long-held assumption about the perfect symmetry of the universe. For this groundbreaking insight, Yang and Lee were awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1957—just one year after their paper was published, making it one of the fastest awards in Nobel history. Their work forever changed our understanding of the cosmos, proving that nature is far more quirky and asymmetrical than we ever imagined.

sources.title: 杨振宁当年发现，次年就获诺奖的宇称不守恒到底是个啥？

articles.headline: Trapped Under the Sky: How a 'Heat Dome' is Cooking Europe and Why Our Climate is Turning Up the Dial
articles.summary:
Imagine putting a lid on a pot of boiling water—the heat has nowhere to go. That is exactly what is happening across Europe right now, except the pot is an entire continent and the lid is a massive high-pressure system in the atmosphere known as a 'heat dome.' This dome acts like a giant invisible cap, trapping warm air close to the Earth's surface. Usually, winds and jet streams would push weather systems along, but right now, this high-pressure lid is stubbornly parked over Europe, constantly compressing the air beneath it and making it hotter.

Why does compressing air make it hotter? It comes down to a cool physics principle called adiabatic warming. When the high-pressure system pushes air downward, the air gets squeezed and compressed. Just like how a bicycle pump gets warm when you use it to push air into a tire, the compressed air in the atmosphere warms up. This hot air tries to rise and cool off, but the high-pressure lid just pushes it back down again. This creates a self-sustaining oven. Meteorologists often call this an 'Omega block' because the jet stream bends around the high pressure in the shape of the Greek letter Omega (Ω)—similar to the teardrop shape seen in weather maps—locking the heat wave in place for days or even weeks.

While heat domes are natural weather phenomena, they are shattering records today because our baseline climate is changing. Global warming means the atmosphere starts off hotter, so when a heat dome forms, the air it compresses is already warmer than it would have been decades ago. Furthermore, the Arctic is warming much faster than the rest of the planet, which slows down the jet stream. A slower jet stream is more likely to wobble and form these extreme, blocking patterns. Think of it like a slow, lazy river that creates big, twisted meanders instead of a fast-flowing stream that pushes things right along.

The result is devastating: record-shattering temperatures that bake cities, dry out rivers, and threaten human health and agriculture. Understanding the mechanics of a heat dome isn't just about passing a science test; it's about recognizing how our atmosphere functions like an engine, and how that engine misfires when we add more greenhouse gases. As these atmospheric 'lids' become hotter and more frequent, adapting to and mitigating climate change is no longer just an option—it's a necessity.

sources.title: Why a ‘heat dome’ over Europe is shattering temperature records right now
